pests.name: Three-lined potato beetle
pests.symptoms_beginner: A slender yellow beetle with three black stripes down its back, often found on tomatillos in particular. The adults and their humpbacked larvae chew ragged holes in the leaves; the larvae carry their own dark excrement on their backs as camouflage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Handpick adults and larvae into soapy water, the most effective control in a home garden. Knock egg clusters off leaf undersides. Neem oil helps with heavy larval pressure.
pests.prevention_beginner: Check plants early and often, especially leaf undersides, and remove the first beetles before they build up. Clearing nightshade weeds nearby removes alternate hosts.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Adults (yellow with three black stripes) and humpbacked larvae skeletonize and hole foliage; larvae mask themselves with frass. Tomatillo is a preferred host.
pests.cause_seasoned: Lema daturaphila (three-lined potato beetle), a chrysomelid leaf beetle specializing on Solanaceae, notably the husk-tomatoes.
pests.cause_beginner: A striped leaf beetle that favors tomatillo and other husk-tomatoes more than it bothers tomato.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick adults, larvae, and orange egg clusters into soapy water. Neem or spinosad for heavy larval populations. Row cover until bloom (then remove for pollinators).
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout early, destroy first arrivals and egg masses, and eliminate volunteer nightshade hosts. Rotation reduces overwintering carryover.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_beginner: Large green caterpillars, up to 4 inches, with a horn on the rear. They strip leaves fast and leave dark pellets of frass below; you often spot the damage before the well-camouflaged caterpillar.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Handpick (a UV flashlight at night makes them glow). Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) is effective on younger larvae. Leave any hornworm covered in white cocoons, those are parasitic wasps doing your work.
pests.prevention_beginner: Till in fall to disrupt overwintering pupae. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering insectary plants. Scout for frass.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata/sexta larvae defoliate rapidly; large green larvae with a caudal horn, frass below feeding sites.
pests.cause_seasoned: Hornworm sphinx-moth larvae, shared across Solanaceae.
pests.cause_beginner: The larva of a large sphinx moth; a few can defoliate a plant quickly.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick; Bt (B. thuringiensis kurstaki) on early instars; spare wasp-parasitized larvae as a biocontrol reservoir.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Fall tillage destroys soil pupae; insectary plantings support Cotesia parasitoids; routine frass scouting.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny black beetles that jump like fleas when disturbed and pepper the leaves with small round shot-holes. Worst on young transplants; established tomatillos shrug off the damage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Floating row cover over young plants, kaolin clay, or spinosad if pressure is heavy. Most established plants outgrow the damage and need no treatment.
pests.prevention_beginner: Protect transplants with row cover early. Keep plants vigorous; clean up nightshade weeds and debris where adults overwinter.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Numerous tiny shot-holes from Epitrix/Phyllotreta adults; thresholds matter mainly at the seedling stage.
pests.cause_seasoned: Solanaceous flea beetles overwintering in debris and field margins.
pests.cause_beginner: Several small Solanaceae-feeding beetles; cosmetic on a vigorous plant but stressful to seedlings.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row cover until established, kaolin clay film, spinosad under heavy pressure.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Early row cover, weed sanitation, and plant vigor; tomatillos tolerate moderate feeding damage.

pests.name: Cutworms
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fat gray-brown caterpillars that hide in the soil by day and chew through the stems of fresh transplants at the soil line overnight, toppling them.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Push a cardboard or foil collar an inch into the soil around each transplant. Handpick at night. Bt or diatomaceous earth around stems helps.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear weeds and crop debris before planting; collars on every transplant; cultivate the bed ahead of setting plants to expose larvae.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Noctuid larvae (Agrotis spp.) sever transplants at the soil line during the establishment window.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cutworm moth larvae in soil and residue.
pests.cause_beginner: Night-feeding moth larvae that sever young stems at ground level.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Stem collars, evening handpicking, Bt, diatomaceous-earth barriers.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Pre-plant weed/residue removal and shallow cultivation; collar each transplant.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects on growing tips and leaf undersides, sometimes with sticky honeydew and ants. Rarely a serious problem on tomatillos.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast off with a water jet; insecticidal soap or neem for stubborn colonies. Marigolds and nasturtiums nearby draw aphid-eating beneficials.
pests.prevention_beginner: Avoid excess nitrogen, which makes the soft growth aphids prefer. Encourage ladybugs and lacewings.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies on new growth and leaf undersides; honeydew and sooty mold possible. Generally minor on this crop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species; populations flush in warm weather.
pests.cause_beginner: Small soft-bodied insects whose numbers can build in warm weather but seldom overwhelm a healthy tomatillo.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Water jet, insecticidal soap or neem on colonies, release or conserve beneficials.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Limit nitrogen, interplant insectary flowers, support natural enemies.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery dusting on the leaves, usually late in the season and in crowded, shaded plantings. It rarely does much harm to a vigorous tomatillo.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Improve airflow by spacing and staking; remove the worst leaves. Potassium-bicarbonate or sulfur sprays help if it spreads.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give plants full sun and wide spacing, and avoid crowding. Good air movement is the main prevention.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery colonies on leaf surfaces, favored by warm days and poor air movement; generally low-impact on this crop.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi (e.g. Leveillula/Oidium); UC notes warm sunny exposure suppresses it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that coats leaf surfaces with white powder in warm, dry conditions with poor airflow.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve canopy airflow, prune affected leaves, apply potassium bicarbonate or sulfur.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Full sun, wide spacing, and staking; avoid dense, shaded plantings.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark brown spots with faint target-like rings on the lower, older leaves, which then yellow and drop. Less common and less damaging on tomatillos than on tomatoes.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove and discard (do not compost) affected leaves. Mulch to stop soil splash. Copper sprays preventively if pressure is high.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rotate away from nightshades for 3 years, water at the base, and stake to keep foliage off the ground.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Concentric-ringed Alternaria lesions on older foliage first, advancing upward; lower incidence than on tomato.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria solani, favored by warm wet conditions and overhead moisture.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soilborne fungus splashed up onto lower leaves in warm, wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation of infected leaves, mulch against splash, preventive copper under pressure.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: 3-year Solanaceae rotation, base watering, staking, airflow.

diseases.name: Mosaic and other viruses
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Mottled light-and-dark green or yellow patches on leaves, sometimes with puckering or stunting. Spread by aphids and by handling.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure: pull and discard infected plants so they do not infect others. Control aphids and wash hands and tools.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy healthy plants, manage aphids, avoid handling plants when wet, and do not use tobacco products near the plants.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Mosaic mottling, leaf distortion, and stunting from mosaic and related viruses; roguing is the only response.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Aphid- and contact-transmitted viruses (TMV/ToMV and others).
diseases.cause_beginner: Plant viruses (including tobacco/tomato mosaic) carried by insects or on hands and tools.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rogue and destroy symptomatic plants; manage aphid vectors; sanitize hands and tools.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Healthy transplants, vector control, tool/hand hygiene, no tobacco contact.

diseases.name: Root and stem rots
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Wilting, blackened lower stems, or sudden collapse, usually where soil stays wet. The most avoidable tomatillo disease, since it comes from soggy ground.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant collapses; remove it. The fix is drainage: never let tomatillos sit in soggy soil.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds, avoid overwatering, and rotate. Tomatillos prefer it on the drier side.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Damping-off, crown/root rot, and wilt from Pythium/Phytophthora/Rhizoctonia in saturated soils.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne oomycetes and fungi favored by waterlogging and poor drainage.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soilborne fungi that attack roots and stems in waterlogged, poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rogue collapsed plants; correct drainage; avoid overwatering this drought-adapted crop.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Well-drained or raised beds, moderate irrigation, rotation away from Solanaceae.
